claim: Freshly isolated mouse alveolar epithelial cells (ATs) comprise a mix of type I cells and type II cells that produce normal surfactant (NS) levels.
source: Freshly isolated mouse ATs comprise a mix of type I cells (Figure 1A) and type II cells that produce normal surfactant (NS) levels (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images in Figure 1A and 1B showing type I and type II cells, and by RT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing expression of surfactant markers.

claim: Prolonged in vitro passage causes ATs to adopt a phenotype with deficient surfactant (DS) levels.
source: Prolonged in vitro passage causes ATs to adopt a phenotype with deficient surfactant (DS) levels (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 1C and RT-PCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A showing reduced expression of surfactant markers after in vitro passage.

claim: DS cells had reduced expression of type II markers such as Abca3 (required for surfactant export) and all four surfactant proteins Sftpa, Sftpb, Sftpc, and Sftpd as measured by RT-PCR.
source: DS cells had reduced expression of type II markers such as Abca3 (required for surfactant export [Beers and Mulugeta, 2017; Besnard et al., 2010]) and all four surfactant proteins Sftpa, Sftpb, Sftpc, and Sftpd (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) as measured by RT-PCR.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and cited literature on Abca3 function.

claim: Abca3 is required for surfactant export.
source: DS cells had reduced expression of type II markers such as Abca3 (required for surfactant export [Beers and Mulugeta, 2017; Besnard et al., 2010])
evidence: Supported by citations to Beers and Mulugeta, 2017 and Besnard et al., 2010.

claim: DS cells showed reduced expression of some type I markers such as Aquaporin (Aqp5) and Podoplanin (Pdpn).
source: These cells also showed reduced expression of some type I markers such as the membrane proteins Aquaporin (Aqp5) and Podoplanin (Pdpn)
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: DS cells had elevated expression of other type I markers such as Caveolin-1 (Cav1) and Insulin Growth Factor Binding Protein 2 (Igfbp2).
source: but had elevated expression of other type I markers such as Caveolin-1 (Cav1) and Insulin Growth Factor Binding Protein 2 (Igfbp2).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The observations are consistent with a majority of the cells in the DS population having a terminal type I phenotype.
source: These observations are consistent with a majority of the cells in this populations having a terminal type I phenotype (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on inference from RT-PCR data and cited literature on type I AT phenotypes.

claim: DS ATs have fewer and smaller lamellar bodies.
source: DS ATs also have fewer and smaller lamellar bodies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data and quantification shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: The low macrophage:AT ratio in the LoC is consistent with alveolar physiology.
source: Typical numbers of ATs, endothelial cells, and macrophages are given in Table 1, the low macrophage: AT ratio is consistent with alveolar physiology (Weibel, 2015).
evidence: Supported by cell density data in Table 1 and citation to Weibel, 2015.

claim: LoCs reconstituted with DS ATs retain deficient surfactant expression on-chip at the ALI with fewer and smaller lamellar bodies detected across multiple fields of view.
source: LoCs reconstituted with DS ATs retain deficient surfactant expression on-chip at the ALI with fewer (Figure 1J) and smaller (Figure 1K) lamellar bodies detected across multiple fields of view.
evidence: Supported by quantification of lamellar bodies in Figure 1J and 1K showing significant differences between NS and DS LoCs.

claim: DS LoCs have reduced expression of some type II markers, notably Abca3, compared to NS LoCs.
source: This phenotype is also reflected in the reduced expression of some type II markers, notably Abca3, in DS LoCs as compared to NS LoCs (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Expression of type I markers including Aqp5 and Pdpn as well as the lung chemokine Cxcl15 was not significantly different between NS and DS LoCs at the ALI.
source: In contrast, expression of type I markers including Aqp5 and Pdpn as well as the lung chemokine Cxcl15 was not significantly different between NS and DS LoCs at the ALI (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 2H.

claim: DS LoCs retained surfactant deficiency for up to 6 days at the ALI.
source: DS LoCs retained surfactant deficiency for up to 6 days at the ALI (Figure 1—figure supplement 2I,J vs. Figure 1—figure supplement 2K,L).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining images in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I-L showing maintained surfactant phenotypes over time.

claim: Inoculation of the LoC with between 200 and 800 Mtb bacilli led to infection of both macrophages and ATs under both NS and DS conditions.
source: Inoculation of the LoC with between 200 and 800 Mtb bacilli led to infection of both macrophages (white boxes in Figure 1M,P, zooms in Figure 1O,R) and ATs (yellow boxes in Figure 1M,P, zooms in Figure 1N,Q) under both NS (Figure 1M–O) and DS (Figure 1P–R) conditions.
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 1M-R showing infected macrophages and ATs.

claim: 7.3% of infected cells (n = 163) isolated from mouse lungs at 8 days post-infection were CD45- pro-SPC+ type II ATs.
source: This revealed that 7.3% of infected cells (n = 163) were CD45- pro-SPC+ type II ATs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–F, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by microscopy analysis of infected mouse lung cells shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A-F and quantified in Figure 1—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Type I AT infection was not found in the mouse lung analysis, likely reflecting challenges in isolating this cell type.
source: We did not find instances of type I AT infection, but this likely reflects the challenges in isolating this cell type.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations and known technical limitations.

claim: The LoC model faithfully reproduces AT infection that also occurs in vivo albeit at a higher frequency.
source: Thus, the LoC model faithfully reproduces AT infection that also occurs in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G) albeit at a higher frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: Supported by comparison of infection frequencies between in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G) and LoC model (Figure 1—figure supplement 3H).

claim: Between 3 and 5 dpi, intracellular growth of Mtb is highly variable in both ATs and macrophages under NS and DS conditions.
source: Between 3 and 5 dpi under NS (Figure 2, A-D, Figure 2—video 1) or DS (Figure 2, E-H, Figure 2—video 2) conditions, intracellular growth of Mtb is highly variable in both ATs (Figure 2I,K) and macrophages (Figure 2J,L).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 2A-L showing variable growth rates.

claim: Bacterial growth is exponential in ATs and macrophages.
source: Plots of the logarithm of total bacterial fluorescence intensity within individual infected cells (representing the spread in growth rates) indicate that bacterial growth is exponential in ATs (Figure 2I,K) and macrophages (Figure 2J,L).
evidence: Supported by linear fits to log-transformed fluorescence intensity data in Figure 2I-L.

claim: Under NS conditions, a substantial fraction of bacteria show very slow growth (doubling time >168 hr) or even a decrease in fluorescence intensity over time, identified as a 'non-growing fraction' (NGF).
source: However, under NS conditions, we identified substantial fraction of bacteria that show very slow growth (doubling time >168 hr) or even a decrease in fluorescence intensity over time. In the absence of a reliable live/dead marker for Mtb, we identify this as a 'non-growing fraction' (NGF).
evidence: Supported by growth rate analysis shown in Figure 2M and defined operationally based on doubling time threshold.

claim: Intracellular bacterial growth is slower in macrophages compared to ATs under NS conditions.
source: Intracellular bacterial growth is slower in macrophages compared to ATs under NS conditions but growth rates in both cell types are equivalent under DS conditions (Figure 2M).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of growth rates shown in Figure 2M (p = 7.8E-8 for NS, p = 0.64 for DS).

claim: Growth rates in both ATs and macrophages are equivalent under DS conditions.
source: Intracellular bacterial growth is slower in macrophages compared to ATs under NS conditions but growth rates in both cell types are equivalent under DS conditions (Figure 2M).
evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of growth rates shown in Figure 2M (p = 0.64 for DS).

claim: Compared to bacterial growth in axenic 7H9 cultures, growth in both cell types is slower under NS conditions.
source: Compared to bacterial growth in axenic 7H9 cultures, growth in both cell types is slower under NS conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but significantly faster under DS conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of growth rate distributions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Compared to bacterial growth in axenic 7H9 cultures, growth in both cell types is significantly faster under DS conditions.
source: Compared to bacterial growth in axenic 7H9 cultures, growth in both cell types is slower under NS conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) but significantly faster under DS conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by comparison of growth rate distributions shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Mtb grows very poorly when cultured axenically in the ALI medium.
source: We also found that Mtb grows very poorly when cultured axenically in the ALI medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 vs Figure 2—figure supplement 4B), which provides indirect evidence that Mtb growth on-chip is likely to be intracellular.
evidence: Supported by growth curve data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: No spatial pattern of intracellular Mtb growth rates was observed within the LoC in both NS and DS conditions.
source: We observed no spatial pattern of intracellular Mtb growth rates within the LoC in both NS and DS conditions, confirming that the observed distributions of growth rates are not due to spatial heterogeneity within the device (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B).
evidence: Supported by 3D spatial plots of growth rates shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A,B.

claim: Surfactant deficiency shifts the host-pathogen equilibrium in favor of Mtb, resulting in uncontrolled bacterial growth even in macrophages.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that surfactant deficiency shifts the host-pathogen equilibrium in favor of Mtb, resulting in uncontrolled bacterial growth even in macrophages.
evidence: Based on inference from growth rate data comparing NS and DS conditions shown in Figure 2M.

claim: The mean growth rate r = 0.78 and mean death rate δ = 0.41 for Mtb replication for the period of days 1–14 post-infection in the mouse model of infection were reported by Gill et al., 2009.
source: Table 1 (Gill et al., 2009) in lists a mean growth rate r = 0.78 and a mean death rate δ = 0.41 for Mtb replication for the period of days 1–14 post-infection in the mouse model of infection.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gill et al., 2009.

claim: The calculated growth rate of 0.022 h−1 from mouse model data is in good agreement with the mean or median growth rate reported for macrophage infections with wild-type Mtb in NS conditions in the LoC model.
source: which is in good agreement with the mean or median growth rate that we report for macrophage infections with wild-type Mtb in NS conditions (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by comparison of calculated value with experimental data in Table 2.

claim: The LoC model provides the entire population distribution of growth rates with an approximately 200-fold higher temporal resolution than mouse models.
source: Notably, the LoC model provides the entire population distribution of growth rates with an approximately 200-fold higher temporal resolution.
evidence: Based on comparison of imaging intervals (1.5-2 hr in LoC) versus typical CFU measurement intervals in mouse models.

claim: Both procedures (treating Mtb or DS LoC with Curosurf) attenuated intracellular Mtb growth and generated a non-growing fraction similar in magnitude to infected NS LoCs.
source: Both procedures attenuated intracellular Mtb growth and generated a non-growing fraction similar in magnitude to infected NS LoCs (Figure 2N, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 2N and Table 2 comparing Curosurf treatments to NS and DS conditions.

claim: Curosurf treatment affects neither Mtb viability nor replication in vitro in the absence of host cells.
source: Curosurf treatment affects neither Mtb viability (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A) nor replication in vitro in the absence of host cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B)
evidence: Supported by CFU data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A and growth curve data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Surfactant protects by altering the interaction of Mtb with host cells rather than by any direct effect on bacterial physiology.
source: suggesting that surfactant protects by altering the interaction of Mtb with host cells rather than by any direct effect on bacterial physiology.
evidence: Based on inference from data showing no direct effect of Curosurf on Mtb viability or growth in the absence of host cells.

claim: Uncontrolled intracellular growth of Mtb in DS LoCs is largely attributable to reduced surfactant secretion.
source: We conclude that uncontrolled intracellular growth of Mtb in DS LoCs is largely attributable to reduced surfactant secretion.
evidence: Based on inference from rescue experiments with exogenous surfactant shown in Figure 2N.

claim: Mtb lacking both the isocitrate lyase genes icl1 and icl2 grows normally under standard conditions in vitro but is incapable of growth in the lungs of mice and is rapidly cleared.
source: Mtb lacking both the isocitrate lyase genes icl1 and icl2 grows normally under standard conditions in vitro but is incapable of growth in the lungs of mice and is rapidly cleared (Muñoz-Elías and McKinney, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muñoz-Elías and McKinney, 2005.

claim: The Δicl1Δicl2 strain is unable to grow in either ATs or macrophages even under the more-permissive DS conditions in the LoC model.
source: In the LoC model, we found that the Δicl1Δicl2 strain is unable to grow in either ATs or macrophages even under the more-permissive DS conditions (Figure 3C vs. A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C for widefield images and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F for confocal images)
evidence: Supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Attenuation of the Δicl1Δicl2 mutant is similar in the LoC and mouse models and independent of surfactant secretion.
source: indicating that attenuation of this mutant is similar in the LoC and mouse models and independent of surfactant secretion.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of LoC data with published mouse model data.

claim: The Δicl1Δicl2 strain has a growth defect relative to wild-type only when intracellular in a host cell due to the accumulation of metabolic intermediates.
source: These results once again are suggestive of intracellular Mtb growth in the LoC model because the Δicl1Δicl2 strain has a growth defect relative to wild-type only when intracellular in a host cell due to the accumulation of metabolic intermediates (Upton and McKinney, 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Upton and McKinney, 2007.

claim: There are no differences in growth between the axenic cultures of Δicl1Δicl2 and wild-type strains in 7H9 medium or in the ALI media used in the LoC experiments.
source: whereas there are no differences in growth between the axenic cultures of Δicl1Δicl2 and wild-type strains in 7H9 medium (Muñoz-Elías and McKinney, 2005) or in the ALI media used in the LoC experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by citation to Muñoz-Elías and McKinney, 2005 and growth curve data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The activity of the ESX-1 Type VII secretion system is upregulated during AT infection.
source: The activity of the ESX-1 Type VII secretion system, a major Mtb virulence factor that is required for escape from the phagosome into the cytosol (van der Wel et al., 2007), is upregulated during AT infection (Ryndak et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to van der Wel et al., 2007 and Ryndak et al., 2015.

claim: The ESX-1 Type VII secretion system is a major Mtb virulence factor that is required for escape from the phagosome into the cytosol.
source: The activity of the ESX-1 Type VII secretion system, a major Mtb virulence factor that is required for escape from the phagosome into the cytosol (van der Wel et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to van der Wel et al., 2007.

claim: Intracellular growth of the ESX-1-deficient strain is largely independent of surfactant levels.
source: In comparison to wild-type Mtb, whose intracellular growth rate is strongly dependent on surfactant levels (Figure 3D–G), intracellular growth of the 5'Tn::pe35 strain (Chen et al., 2013) that is deficient in ESX-1 secretion but retains PDIM secretion (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) is largely independent of surfactant levels (Figure 3H–K).
evidence: Supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 3H-K comparing NS and DS conditions for ESX-1-deficient strain.

claim: Under NS conditions, a greater fraction of ESX-1-deficient bacteria are 'non-growing' in ATs.
source: Under NS conditions, a greater fraction of ESX-1-deficient bacteria are 'non-growing' in ATs (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by NGF data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Under DS conditions, the ESX-1-deficient strain is unable to grow as rapidly as wild-type in both macrophages and ATs.
source: Under DS conditions, the ESX-1-deficient strain is unable to grow as rapidly as wild-type in both macrophages and ATs (Figure 4B,D)
evidence: Supported by growth rate comparison data shown in Figure 4B,D.

claim: Under DS conditions, approximately 12% of ESX-1-deficient bacteria are non-growing in macrophages.
source: and a fraction (ca. 12%) of ESX-1-deficient bacteria are non-growing in macrophages (Figure 3K).
evidence: Supported by NGF data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Macrophages are less permissive than ATs for intracellular growth of ESX-1-deficient Mtb under both NS and DS conditions.
source: Macrophages are less permissive than ATs for intracellular growth of ESX-1-deficient Mtb under both NS and DS conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by growth rate comparison data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Wild-type Mtb grows more slowly in macrophages than in ATs only under NS but not DS conditions.
source: In contrast, wild-type Mtb, grows more slowly in macrophages than in ATs only under NS but not DS conditions (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by growth rate comparison data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Attenuation of ESX-1-deficient bacteria relative to wild-type is not rescued by surfactant deficiency.
source: Overall, attenuation of ESX-1-deficient bacteria relative to wild-type is not rescued by surfactant deficiency.
evidence: Based on inference from growth rate data comparing ESX-1-deficient and wild-type strains under NS and DS conditions.

claim: ESX-1 secretion is necessary for rapid intracellular growth in the absence of surfactant.
source: This demonstrates that ESX-1 secretion is necessary for rapid intracellular growth in the absence of surfactant, consistent with the hypothesis that surfactant may attenuate Mtb growth by depleting ESX-1 components on the bacterial cell surface (Raffetseder et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on inference from ESX-1-deficient strain data and cited hypothesis from Raffetseder et al., 2019.

claim: Surfactant may attenuate Mtb growth by depleting ESX-1 components on the bacterial cell surface.
source: consistent with the hypothesis that surfactant may attenuate Mtb growth by depleting ESX-1 components on the bacterial cell surface (Raffetseder et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raffetseder et al., 2019 and inference from experimental data.

claim: At 2 dpi, population sizes for the ESX-1-deficient strains are significantly smaller than for wild-type Mtb in simulations.
source: At 2 dpi, population sizes for the ESX-1-deficient strains (Figure 4E, n = 100, p=2.3×10−6) are already significantly smaller than for wild-type Mtb.
evidence: Supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The levels of attenuation predicted by simulations using values from NS LoC conditions are in good agreement with experimental data from the mouse model in the acute phase of infection.
source: The levels of attenuation predicted by this simple model using values from NS (Figure 4F) but not DS (Figure 4G) LoC conditions are in good agreement with the experimental data for both mutants from the mouse model in the acute phase of infection (Chen et al., 2013; Rao et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by comparison of simulation results in Figure 4F with published mouse model data from Chen et al., 2013 and Rao et al., 2005.

claim: Surfactant secretion by freshly isolated ATs in NS conditions in the LoC model provides a better mimic of the native lung environment than DS conditions.
source: These results provide a strong validation that surfactant secretion by freshly isolated ATs in NS conditions in the LoC model provide a better mimic of the native lung environment than DS conditions and serve to benchmark the LoC model.
evidence: Based on inference from agreement between NS LoC simulations and mouse model data.

claim: Surfactant still has a small but significant impact on growth of ESX-1-deficient Mtb in macrophages.
source: Although attenuation of the ESX-1-deficient strain is completely independent of surfactant in ATs (Figure 3H,I), surfactant still has a small but significant impact on growth of ESX-1-deficient Mtb in macrophages (Figure 3J,K).
evidence: Supported by growth rate data shown in Figure 3J,K showing statistical significance (p=5.1E-3).

claim: Surfactant readily coated the bacteria, albeit heterogeneously.
source: microscopic examination of Mtb exposed to fluorescently labeled Curosurf with a fluorescent analogue of DPPC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) revealed that surfactant readily coated the bacteria (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–E), albeit heterogeneously (compare Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C with Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: Supported by microscopy images in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E showing surfactant coating on bacteria.

claim: Curosurf partially strips the Mtb cell surface of sulfoglycolipids (SGL).
source: We found that Curosurf partially strips the Mtb cell surface of sulfoglycolipids (SGL) (Figure 5C,E)
evidence: Supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5C,E showing reduced SGL in surfactant-treated samples.

claim: Curosurf partially strips the Mtb cell surface of trehalose dimycolate (TDM).
source: and trehalose dimycolate (TDM) (Figure 5D,E)
evidence: Supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5D,E showing reduced TDM in surfactant-treated samples.

claim: Curosurf does not strip phthiocerol dimycocerosates (PDIM) from the Mtb cell surface.
source: but not phthiocerol dimycocerosates (PDIM) (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by TLC data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing no change in PDIM levels.

claim: The surfactant-mediated removal of virulence-associated lipids suggests an additional mechanism for the attenuation of intracellular growth of Mtb in macrophages.
source: The surfactant-mediated removal of these virulence-associated lipids (Dulberger et al., 2020) suggests an additional mechanism for the attenuation of intracellular growth of Mtb in macrophages.
evidence: Based on inference from lipid stripping data and citation to Dulberger et al., 2020 on virulence-associated lipids.

claim: Due to the small diameter of respiratory bronchioles only the smallest aerosol droplets containing one to two bacilli are successfully transported to the alveolar space.
source: due to the small diameter of respiratory bronchioles only the smallest aerosol droplets containing one to two bacilli are successfully transported to the alveolar space (Ma and Darquenne, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ma and Darquenne, 2011.

claim: The 'first contact' with a naive host is by default a single-cell interaction between an Mtb bacillus and a host cell.
source: and the 'first contact' with a naive host is by default a single-cell interaction between an Mtb bacillus and a host cell.
evidence: Based on inference from aerosol deposition characteristics cited from Ma and Darquenne, 2011.

claim: There is some evidence that pulmonary surfactant plays host-protective role in early Mtb interactions.
source: There is some evidence that pulmonary surfactant plays host-protective role in these early interactions (Torrelles and Schlesinger, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Torrelles and Schlesinger, 2017.

claim: A complete understanding of the role of surfactant is difficult to obtain from animal infection models owing to the lethality of surfactant deficiency.
source: but a complete understanding of the role of surfactant is difficult to obtain from animal infection models owing to the lethality of surfactant deficiency.
evidence: Based on knowledge of the essential role of surfactant in lung function.

claim: Experiments in animal models cannot provide information about the dynamics of host-Mtb interactions at early stage with sufficient spatiotemporal resolution.
source: In addition, experiments in animal models (Collins and Orme, 1994) cannot provide information about the dynamics of host-Mtb interactions at this early stage with sufficient spatiotemporal resolution (Westphalen et al., 2014; Looney et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Collins and Orme, 1994; Westphalen et al., 2014; and Looney et al., 2011.

claim: Infection of macrophages with Mtb has been used to probe the role of certain surfactant components.
source: A commonly used in vitro model, infection of macrophages with Mtb (Lerner et al., 2017), has been used to probe the role of certain surfactant components (Arcos et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lerner et al., 2017 and Arcos et al., 2011.

claim: Macrophage infection studies cannot address the role of native surfactant secreted by alveolar epithelial cells at an air-liquid interface.
source: but these studies cannot address the role of native surfactant secreted by alveolar epithelial cells (ATs) at an air-liquid interface (ALI), a condition that has been reported to alter Mtb physiology (Ojha et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on inference from limitations of macrophage-only models and citation to Ojha et al., 2008 on ALI effects.

claim: Air-liquid interface conditions have been reported to alter Mtb physiology.
source: a condition that has been reported to alter Mtb physiology (Ojha et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ojha et al., 2008.

claim: Organ-on-chip systems have emerged as crucial tools for the replacement of animal models in drug development, toxicity testing, and personalized medicine.
source: These systems have emerged as crucial tools for the replacement of animal models in drug development, toxicity testing, and personalized medicine (Ghaemmaghami et al., 2012; Ronaldson-Bouchard and Vunjak-Novakovic, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ghaemmaghami et al., 2012 and Ronaldson-Bouchard and Vunjak-Novakovic, 2018.

claim: Organ-on-chip systems can combine key advantages of both simpler in vitro models and animal models.
source: where they can combine key advantages of both simpler in vitro models and animal models (Torrelles and Schlesinger, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Torrelles and Schlesinger, 2017.

claim: ATs are the major cellular component of the distal lung.
source: ATs are the major cellular component of the distal lung
evidence: Based on established knowledge of lung anatomy.

claim: Despite sporadic reports of AT infection in human TB, the role of ATs remains controversial.
source: yet despite sporadic reports of AT infection in human TB (Barrios-Payán et al., 2012; Hernández-Pando et al., 2000), the role of ATs remains controversial.
evidence: Supported by citations to Barrios-Payán et al., 2012 and Hernández-Pando et al., 2000.

claim: Previous work has revealed the specific roles of hydrophilic SP-A and SP-D proteins in altering the uptake and intracellular processing of Mtb in macrophages.
source: Previous work has revealed the specific roles of hydrophilic SP-A and SP-D proteins (Ferguson et al., 2006; Pasula et al., 1997) in altering the uptake and intracellular processing of Mtb in macrophages.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferguson et al., 2006 and Pasula et al., 1997.

claim: Surfactant hydrolase enzymes within the alveolar lining fluid have been shown to release Mtb cell wall fragments as well as alter Mtb growth in ATs.
source: Surfactant hydrolase enzymes within the alveolar lining fluid Arcos et al., 2011; Scordo et al., 2017 have also been shown to release Mtb cell wall fragments as well as alter Mtb growth in ATs.
evidence: Supported by citations to Arcos et al., 2011 and Scordo et al., 2017.

claim: For the most part, specific components of surfactant can suppress intracellular Mtb growth.
source: Together, these studies show that, for the most part, specific components of surfactant can suppress intracellular Mtb growth.
evidence: Based on inference from cited studies on surfactant components.

claim: Surfactant lipids have been reported to upregulate Mtb growth via increased expression of CD36.
source: However, surfactant lipids have also been reported to upregulate Mtb growth via increased expression of CD36 (Dodd et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dodd et al., 2016.

claim: The alveolar lining fluid from some patients has been shown to increase intracellular replication in epithelial cells and exacerbate infection.
source: and the alveolar lining fluid from some patients has also been shown to increase intracellular replication in epithelial cells and exacerbate infection (Scordo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scordo et al., 2019.

claim: All previous studies focused on the role of specific components of surfactant and none probed the role of endogenous surfactant expression in co-cultures maintained at the ALI.
source: However, all these studies focused on the role of specific components of surfactant and none of these studies probed the role of endogenous surfactant expression in co-cultures maintained at the ALI.
evidence: Based on review of cited literature.

claim: The unexpectedly rapid and uncontrolled intracellular growth of Mtb at the ALI in the absence of surfactant has not been reported previously in simpler in vitro models of host cell infection.
source: The unexpectedly rapid and uncontrolled intracellular growth of Mtb at the ALI in the absence of surfactant has not been reported previously in simpler in vitro models of host cell infection.
evidence: Based on review of literature and comparison with current findings.

claim: Under NS conditions, a substantial non-growing fraction of intracellular Mtb was identified in both ATs and macrophages, which may be equivalent to the 'non-growing but metabolically active' (NGMA) populations previously observed in the lungs of mice.
source: Under NS conditions, we identified a substantial non-growing fraction of intracellular Mtb in both ATs and macrophages, which may be equivalent to the 'non-growing but metabolically active' (NGMA) populations previously observed in the lungs of mice (Manina et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from NGF data and citation to Manina et al., 2015.

claim: Pulmonary surfactant plays an important role in host innate immunity during early Mtb infection.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that pulmonary surfactant plays an important role in host innate immunity during early Mtb infection
evidence: Based on inference from all experimental findings in the study.

claim: Individuals with defective surfactant function show an increased risk of developing active TB.
source: which may partly explain why individuals with defective surfactant function (Finley and Ladman, 1972; Subramaniam et al., 1995; Moliva et al., 2019) also show an increased risk of developing active TB.
evidence: Supported by citations to Finley and Ladman, 1972; Subramaniam et al., 1995; and Moliva et al., 2019.

claim: Smokers and elderly persons with compromised surfactant function are at increased risk of developing active tuberculosis.
source: These findings may partly explain why smokers and elderly persons with compromised surfactant function are at increased risk of developing active tuberculosis.
evidence: Based on inference from study findings and general knowledge about risk factors for TB.

claim: ATs are more permissive to Mtb growth than macrophages under NS (but not DS) conditions.
source: We also report that ATs are more permissive to Mtb growth than macrophages under NS (but not DS) conditions.
evidence: Supported by growth rate comparison data in Figure 2M and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Infection of ATs is not an artefact of the LoC model, as infected ATs were also identified in the lungs of aerosol-infected mice using a sensitive microscopy-based approach.
source: Infection of ATs is not an artefact of the LoC model, as we also identified infected ATs in the lungs of aerosol-infected mice using a sensitive microscopy-based approach, which might be more discriminating than FACS-based approaches used previously (Cohen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by microscopy data from mouse lungs in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citation to Cohen et al., 2018.

claim: Alveolar macrophages in the lung have been shown to be sessile.
source: Alveolar macrophages in the lung have been shown to be sessile (Westphalen et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Westphalen et al., 2014.

claim: The higher incidence of AT infection in the LoC model is probably due to differences in the method of Mtb inoculation.
source: and so the higher incidence of AT infection in the LoC model is probably due to differences in the method of Mtb inoculation.
evidence: Based on inference from comparison of LoC inoculation method with aerosol infection in mice.

claim: Most infected individuals harbor just one primary lesion originating from a single bacillus.
source: Given the very low inoculum size in human Mtb (most infected individuals harbor just one primary lesion originating from a single bacillus Mckinney et al., 1998)
evidence: Supported by citation to Mckinney et al., 1998.

claim: First contact with an AT, albeit much rarer in vivo, could potentially lead to a more aggressive infection.
source: we speculate that first contact with an AT, albeit much rarer in vivo could potentially lead to a more aggressive infection.
evidence: Based on speculation from experimental findings showing ATs are more permissive than macrophages under NS conditions.

claim: The proportion of exposed individuals who develop clinical TB is low.
source: This could provide one explanation for the observation that the proportion of exposed individuals who develop clinical TB is low.
evidence: Based on general knowledge about TB epidemiology.

claim: Time-lapse imaging at an ALI in the LoC infection model directly quantifies bacterial growth rates with a spatiotemporal resolution that is unachievable using indirect measurements of bacterial growth rates in mouse models of TB.
source: Time-lapse imaging at an ALI in the LoC infection model directly quantifies bacterial growth rates with a spatiotemporal resolution that is unachievable using indirect measurements of bacterial growth rates in mouse models of TB (e.g. plating tissue homogenates to measure colony-forming units [CFU]).
evidence: Based on comparison of imaging intervals in LoC versus CFU measurement intervals in mouse models.

claim: The deliberate choice to use murine over human cells allows addition of macrophages from a mouse line that constitutively expresses GFP, providing unambiguous identification of these cells over multiple days.
source: The deliberate choice to use murine over human cells allows us to add macrophages to the chip from a mouse line that constitutively expresses GFP, and provides unambiguous identification of these cells over multiple days which would not be possible with CellTracker and other fluorescent dyes.
evidence: Based on experimental design rationale and knowledge of fluorescent labeling methods.

claim: Average growth rates for wild-type Mtb under NS conditions are in good agreement with net Mtb growth rates measured using a plasmid-loss assay in mice.
source: For example, average growth rates for wild-type Mtb under NS conditions are in good agreement with net Mtb growth rates measured using a plasmid-loss assay in mice (Gill et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by comparison of LoC data with data from Gill et al., 2009.

claim: The microscopy-based approach reveals the population distribution of growth rates, which highlights that even under NS conditions, a small proportion of cells show robust intracellular Mtb growth.
source: However, our microscopy-based approach also reveals the population distribution of growth rates, which highlights that even under NS conditions, a small proportion of cells show robust intracellular Mtb growth
evidence: Supported by growth rate distribution data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Robust and attenuated Mtb growth can occur in close proximity to each other on-chip.
source: and that robust and attenuated Mtb growth can occur in close proximity to each other on-chip.
evidence: Supported by spatial analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: These observations reinforce an important role for cell-to-cell heterogeneity in host-Mtb outcomes.
source: These observations reinforce an important role for cell-to-cell heterogeneity in host-Mtb outcomes (Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on inference from growth rate heterogeneity data and citation to Lin et al., 2014.

claim: The growth characteristics of ESX-1-deficient Mtb in the LoC model are in agreement with experiments from animal models, further validating the LoC model.
source: The growth characteristics of ESX-1-deficient Mtb in our LoC model are also in agreement with experiments from animal models, further validating the LoC model.
evidence: Based on comparison of LoC data with published animal model data.

claim: Curosurf is a surfactant replacement formulation of phospholipids and hydrophobic proteins.
source: Exogenous addition of Curosurf, a surfactant replacement formulation of phospholipids and hydrophobic proteins, rescues the effects of surfactant deficiency on mycobacterial growth to a large extent.
evidence: Based on knowledge of Curosurf composition.

claim: Phospholipids are the main component of native surfactant.
source: Phospholipids are the main component of native surfactant
evidence: Based on established knowledge of surfactant composition.

claim: Lipid recycling is a key function of type II ATs and alveolar macrophages.
source: and lipid recycling is a key function of type II ATs and alveolar macrophages (Olmeda et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Olmeda et al., 2017.

claim: The two-way interaction of surfactant with the bacterial cell surface may alter how host cells take up these bacteria, or how they are processed after uptake.
source: The two-way interaction of surfactant with the bacterial cell surface (surfactant removes virulence-associated Mtb surface lipids and proteins, and surfactant lipids coat the Mtb surface) may alter how host cells take up these bacteria, or how they are processed after uptake.
evidence: Based on speculation from experimental findings on surfactant-bacteria interactions.

claim: Surfactant phospholipids have been shown to have antiviral properties and can serve as a potent adjuvant for antiviral vaccines either on their own or as a medium for delivery of immune-stimulating molecules to ATs.
source: More generally, surfactant phospholipids have been shown to have antiviral properties and can serve as a potent adjuvant for antiviral vaccines either on their own (Kimoto et al., 2013) or as a medium for delivery of immune-stimulating molecules to ATs (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kimoto et al., 2013 and Wang et al., 2020.

claim: The findings suggest a potential role for pulmonary surfactant replacement formulations in host-directed therapies against TB.
source: Our findings suggest a potential role for pulmonary surfactant replacement formulations in host-directed therapies against TB.
evidence: Based on speculation from experimental findings showing surfactant rescue of DS phenotype.

claim: These insights were made possible by use of an organ-on-chip system that reproduces host physiology in a modular and tuneable fashion, which is frequently impossible to achieve in vivo.
source: These insights were made possible by use of an organ-on-chip system that reproduces host physiology in a modular and tuneable fashion, which is frequently impossible to achieve in vivo.
evidence: Based on inference from the advantages of the LoC model demonstrated throughout the study.

claim: Surfactant deficiency results in rapid and uncontrolled bacterial growth in both macrophages and alveolar epithelial cells.
source: Surfactant deficiency results in rapid and uncontrolled bacterial growth in both macrophages and alveolar epithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by growth rate data comparing NS and DS conditions in Figure 2M.

claim: Under normal surfactant levels, a significant fraction of intracellular bacteria are non-growing.
source: In contrast, under normal surfactant levels, a significant fraction of intracellular bacteria are non-growing.
evidence: Supported by NGF data in Figure 2M and Figure 3.

claim: The surfactant-deficient phenotype is rescued by exogenous addition of surfactant replacement formulations, which have no effect on bacterial viability in the absence of host cells.
source: The surfactant-deficient phenotype is rescued by exogenous addition of surfactant replacement formulations, which have no effect on bacterial viability in the absence of host cells.
evidence: Supported by rescue data in Figure 2N and viability data in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Surfactant partially removes virulence-associated lipids and proteins from the bacterial cell surface.
source: Surfactant partially removes virulence-associated lipids and proteins from the bacterial cell surface.
evidence: Supported by TLC data in Figure 5C-E showing removal of SGL and TDM.

claim: The attenuation of bacteria lacking the ESX-1 secretion system is independent of surfactant levels.
source: Consistent with this mechanism, the attenuation of bacteria lacking the ESX-1 secretion system is independent of surfactant levels.
evidence: Supported by growth rate data for ESX-1-deficient strain in Figure 3H-K showing similar attenuation in NS and DS conditions.
